title: Spokane-raised Author Devon Kelley brings new PNW cryptid book to Auntie's
excerpt: At the edge of the forest near Mount St. Helens, the wind may carry the ghoulish howls of something lurking in the shadows. Mysteriously large footprints hidden within the brush
content:
At the edge of the forest near Mount St. Helens, the wind may carry the ghoulish howls of something lurking in the shadows. Mysteriously large footprints hidden within the brush could belong to a bear or perhaps something much bigger.

The area of southwest Washington is infamous for alleged mythical creature sightings and, for Spokane-born author Devon Kelley, it sounds like the perfect place for a cryptid-hunting excursion.

“It’s kind of like the one-stop shop for me,” says the author of Cryptids of the Pacific Northwest: The Pend Oreille Paddler, Ringdocus, and the Iconic Sasquatch.

From listening for Sasquatch noises and catching ghosts in motion to scouring the skies for UFO sightings, Kelley has spent years digging into the lore behind unknown creatures spotted around the Pacific Northwest. But her new book isn’t a simple field guide to monster spotting.

Over the course of six months, Kelley dug through newspaper archives, books, blogs and museum collections to track down where some of the Pacific Northwest’s strangest creature stories began — and how they’ve evolved via oral tradition, newspapers and catalogs, eventually cementing their popularity worldwide.

Kelley learned about plenty of human-made hoaxes during her research, but she also came across information that made her reconsider what exactly qualifies as a cryptid. 

She dove deep into cryptozoology, the technically pseudoscientific study of animals whose existence is disputed or not yet scientifically documented. The term “cryptid” originally referred to creatures believed to exist but not yet confirmed by science, such as the Loch Ness Monster or animals thought to be extinct but still reported as seen by witnesses.

Over time, the definition has expanded to include paranormal and pop-culture creatures such as Mothman, a humanoid creature with glowing red eyes and moth-like wings said to have been first spotted in West Virginia in the 1960s. For Kelley, that evolution into culture is part of what makes the subject so interesting, especially as a divide remains between some within the cryptozoology community and those who embrace cryptids as a part of the paranormal.

She first gained interest in the unexplained during childhood when she watched a PBS documentary about the thylacine, also known as the Tasmanian tiger. The striped, wolf-like marsupial was declared extinct in 1986, though reports of people seeing it continued for decades. No living thylacine has ever been scientifically confirmed, but the possibility that an animal could disappear from the scientific record while continuing to be spotted drew Kelley’s interest.

Eventually she began sharing these stories with others who shared her curiosity.

The Ouija Broads: Tales from the Pacific Northweird is a podcast Kelley has co-hosted with Liz Wood since 2017. The show explores the region’s stranger stories, from ghosts and forgotten history to, yes, cryptids.

Now Kelley has expanded on that storytelling with Cryptids of the Pacific Northwest, which dives notably deeper than her podcast could while also exploring the zoological arguments surrounding some of the region’s most well-known cryptids. The book includes chapters on the Pend Oreille Paddler, a lake monster inhabiting Lake Pend Oreille, and the Ringdocus, a large wolf-like cryptid killed in Montana in 1886 that was never DNA tested but remains displayed at the Madison Valley History Museum in Ennis, Montana. 

Kelley was less interested in simply collecting a bunch of monster stories — she wanted to figure out how the stories came to be in the first place. And the answers weren’t just sitting online. 

“There’s more in my book than you’ll ever see online, no matter how much you Google,” she says. “Because this information doesn’t exist online. It exists in a library or in a museum database.”

Her research also brought her to stories connected to Indigenous communities.

Kelley consulted Lindsay Ravensong, an artist and storyteller of Native descent, about how to acknowledge those stories without speaking for communities she isn’t part of. Rather than presenting such figures as cryptids, Kelley includes information about their cultural origins and directs readers toward the communities themselves.

“When a story is removed from its culture of origin, you miss all of the nuance,” she says. “You can miss all of the allegory. You can miss all of the teaching that was supposed to go along with this story.”

She points to the Harrison Hot Springs Visitor Centre & Sasquatch Museum in British Columbia as an example. Opened in 2024, the museum was designed to honor the Indigenous and historical roots of the region, with its dedicated Sts’ailes Longhouse Room highlighting the cultural heritage of the local Sts’ailes First Nation. Alongside exhibits exploring Sasquatch lore, witness accounts, myths and scientific theories, the museum gives visitors a chance to understand the creature beyond the question of whether it could be a zoological discovery.

For Kelley, the different ways people understand cryptids don’t have to cancel each other out. Some reported creatures are probably misidentified animals. Others, she thinks, could represent animals science hasn’t yet documented.

But her belief isn’t rooted in one piece of evidence that convinced her.

“More than anything, I believe in cryptids because I want to believe in cryptids,” Kelley says. “It is my own desire to see the world as interesting, as mysterious, as a little spooky, as a little creepy, as very special.”

That sense of wonder is ultimately what she hopes readers find in the book. Not necessarily proof of a monster hiding in the woods, but another reason to pay closer attention to the place around them.

“I want people to see cryptids as a mascot for where you live,” Kelley says. “I’m not into sports. I’m hella into cryptids. I can see Sasquatch as hometown pride, as an emblem of where I live, as a symbol of the weird and the wonderful that is the Pacific Northwest.”

So if you’re ever wandering around the forest and hear something moving through the trees, it might be worth taking a closer look. You never know what you might find lurking in the Pacific Northweird.
